selectedCourseReview.name: Personal & Professional Development
selectedCourseReview.actualContent: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate student formation, namely, actively, consciously and ethically relating to oneself, others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhances critical thinking and independent learning. It also helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners. The course stimulates core academic skills, namely: Select and critically analyze academic sources Articulate research questions, thesis statements and arguments Improve communication skills through various forms of writing and speaking activities The course fosters personal, social and civic competencies, namely: Craft own academic and personal learning goals Critically reflect on own learning Develop effective collaborative learning approaches with peers, instructors and external partners Valuing community engagement, including the value of different knowledge types and perspectives
selectedCourseReview.contribution: MandatoryYear1PPD

selectedCourseReview.name: Introduction to Economics
selectedCourseReview.actualContent: This course provides an introduction to the principles of economics. The first part of the course delves into microeconomics concepts, including supply and demand, game theory, theory of consumer behaviour, theory of the firm and market structure. The seco nd part of the course covers macroeconomics, beginning with an exploration of macroeconomics events and fundamental concepts such as aggregate output, unemployment and inflation rate. It then examines the dynamics of goods and financial markets in the short run.
selectedCourseReview.contribution: introduces the economics of markets and national economies relevant to globalisation and urban change

selectedCourseReview.name: International Macroeconomics
selectedCourseReview.actualContent: This course explores the economy as a whole by examining its dynamics over the short, medium, and long run. Key indicators such as national income, economic growth, inflation, and unemployment are studied. The course analyses how fiscal and monetary polici es affect the economy. It also covers business cycles, economic crises, and international trade, providing the tools needed to interpret economic data, evaluate policy decisions, and understand global economic trends.
selectedCourseReview.contribution: studies international trade and macroeconomic trends, linking global economic change to policy

selectedCourseReview.name: Public Economics
selectedCourseReview.actualContent: This course examines the role of government in the economy, focusing on how public policy affects efficiency and equity. It explores the rationale for government intervention and key concepts such as market failure, public goods, externalities, taxation, p ublic spending, redistribution, and political economy. By combining theoretical models with empirical evidence, the course provides a framework for analysing the economic impact of public policies.
selectedCourseReview.contribution: analyses government intervention, public goods and externalities relevant to environmental and urban policy

selectedCourseReview.name: Econometrics
selectedCourseReview.actualContent: Econometrics supplies tools to analyze data to answer questions of causality and prediction. In this course you learn three estimators—Ordinary Least Squares, Generalized Least Squares, and Instrumental Variables—and three tests—t-test, F-test, and LM-test. Understanding the basic rules of econometrics, particularly the sampling distribution concept, is key, and the course uses Monte Carlo simulations in Stata to visualize it. Tools are applied to estimate economic relationships and make predictions, and students write an empirical paper.
selectedCourseReview.contribution: uses econometric inference and an empirical paper to assess policy and social-economic relationships

selectedCourseReview.name: Research Methods & Statistics
selectedCourseReview.actualContent: Research Methods & Statistics is a general introduction in research methodology and statistics. The introduction to methodology includes the logics and design of research (e.g., operationalization, experimental design, sampling), and some specific techniques (e.g., laboratory research, surveys). The introduction to statistics includes descriptive and inferential statistics, covering measures of central tendency, spread, association, univariate and bivariate inferential statistics, and analysis of variance. This course includes an introduction to simple applications of multivariate statistics but most coverage of multivariate statistics and statistical modelling will be covered in the course HCBPSYC211 Statistics & Experimental Methods in Health & Behavioral Sciences. The first 9 course weeks (not including the semester break) of the course provide the theoretical background. This includes not only instruction and practice in basic research methodology and statistics, but also the planning stages of the group research projects that will dominate the latter portion of the semester. In this portion of the semester, students of each section attend two classes each week with their instructor. Project groups are formed, and these groups work together in applying newly learned concepts to their own research problem thru individually completed homework exercises, and through sharing and discussing their progress with the rest of the class. The final 6 course weeks are dedicated exclusively to group project work. This research project can fall within any academic discipline.
selectedCourseReview.contribution: develops statistical and research skills for examining social and economic change

selectedCourseReview.name: Introduction to Data Science
selectedCourseReview.actualContent: Data science provides tools for extracting meaningful information from data. In this course, you develop foundational abilities in data visualization as well as data cleaning and manipulation. Next to traditional data coming in the form of tables, we explore non-traditional data types such as spatial data and text data. The course includes much hands -on work with example data sets coming from sciences, social sciences, and arts and humanities. At the end of the course, you carry out your own research project in which you apply your data analysis and visualization skills to answer a research question.
selectedCourseReview.contribution: develops data analysis and visualisation useful for quantitative investigation; it does not teach geographic GIS methods

selectedCourseReview.name: Building with Nature
selectedCourseReview.actualContent: Building, or the construction of man-made structures, would seem to be at odds with nature. One is shaped over time by natural forces, while the other makes changes to suit our specific human needs at a given time. However, to truly stand the test of time human structures, and thus to some degree civilisation, must work with nature and not in spite of it, or even against it. In this course we will explore different aspects of Building with Nature, with special interest in those aspects of Zeeland where this approach has been implemented. We will also explore a bit of the history of Walcheren to better understand what situations its people have already overcome, when facing the sea. Furthermore, we will look at how better planning and engineering is allowing nature to maintain, or even regain, vital ecosystem health across the globe. How can we learn from nature and utilise the forces at work to our mutual benefit? How can we make space for ourselves without disrupting key habitat features animals depend on to thrive?
selectedCourseReview.contribution: studies how built structures and coastal planning work with natural processes in Zeeland

selectedCourseReview.name: Living with Water
selectedCourseReview.actualContent: Delta regions around the world face growing challenges related to sea-level rise, flooding, freshwater scarcity, land subsidence, and unequal access to water and protection. At the same time, these regions are home to millions of people whose lives are shaped by water. This course explores how societies in delta regions manage water risks and opportunities, with a particular focus on the Dutch province of Zeeland as a living laboratory. Students are introduced to key concepts in sustainable water management, including flood protection, drainage and freshwater management, salinization, land subsidence, the ecological consequences of water infrastructure, and the social dimensions of water governance. The course examines how historical events have shaped contemporary approaches to water management, and how governance structures, laws, and institutions influence decisions about safety, land use, sustainability, and whose interests are prioritized. Throughout the course, emphasis is placed on the idea of adapting to water dynamics through integrated strategies, nature-based solutions, and resilient planning, while critically reflecting on questions of long-term social impacts. Learning takes place through a combination of assigned readings, short lectures, group discussions, and in-class activities that encourage critical reflection and collaborative learning. Students engage with real-world cases through guest speakers from policy and research, as well as excursions and field-based activities in Zeeland when possible.
selectedCourseReview.contribution: examines delta water risks and the social dimensions of water governance

selectedCourseReview.name: R3: Recycling, Recovery, Remediation
selectedCourseReview.actualContent: Examines strategies and technologies towards a circular economy. Explores resource security and stewardship, develops lab skills and inorganic chemistry knowledge, and connects to themes at the Delta Climate Center.
selectedCourseReview.contribution: examines recycling, recovery and remediation technologies for circular resource management

selectedCourseReview.name: Governance of Sustainability
selectedCourseReview.actualContent: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions. The first part of this course introduces you to the basic conceptual tools for understanding governance and to the major fault line in tackling sustainability problems as identified by Charles Mann in “The Wizard and the Prophet”. Wizards are techno-optimists who believe humanity’s creativity can tackle every challenge, whilst Prophets argue that humans should take a holistic and systemic approach that calls for a drastic reduction of exploiting the earth resources to respect planetary boundaries. In the second part of the course, we use Problem Based Learning to examine governance solutions to concrete sustainability challenges regarding food, freshwater, energy, and climate change.
selectedCourseReview.contribution: analyses local, national and international sustainability policy and collective decision-making

selectedCourseReview.name: Introduction to Biodiversity
selectedCourseReview.actualContent: The biosphere consists of millions of living species, and millions more have existed in the past. The total number of living species is still unknown, but current developments in palaeontology, molecular biology, and sampling techniques, have reshaped our view of the classification of the living world. It is now recognized that plants and animals; traditionally the two groups defining the science of biology, are merely two branches on a giant tree of life. Many other independent and diverse groups exist, such as brown algae, fungi, diatoms, archaea and many different groups of bacteria. The aim of this course is two-fold. Firstly, it will provide an overview of the living world. We will travel through the tree of life, starting with the prokaryote domains of bacteria and archaea. We will investigate different prokaryote groups, their ways of life, and their manifestations in the world around us. Next, we will explore the diversity of eukaryotes. There are countless single-celled eukaryotic groups that play important ecological roles, such as dinoflagellates that help create coral reefs, and apicomplexans that cause diseases like malaria. Finally, we will discuss the multicellular groups that shape the world around us: plants, seaweeds, fungi and animals. Methods for investigating biodiversity will also be discussed. The second aim of this course is to investigate the relevance of biodiversity for human society. There are multiple number domains in which biodiversity is important, i.e.
selectedCourseReview.contribution: introduces biodiversity as an ecological foundation for environmental decisions

selectedCourseReview.name: Conservation Biology
selectedCourseReview.actualContent: There have been many extinction events in earth’s history, including 5 mass extinctions, where at least 70% of species have died out. These have all been the result of global changes in climate and habitat, due to large catastrophic events or major shifts in atmospheric composition. We are currently on the cusp of a 6th mass extinction, the Holocene mass extinction. However, this one is caused by the actions of a single species: Homo sapiens. Our actions have both directly (overhunting/fishing) or indirectly (climate change, habitat destruction) caused many species to already go extinct, and brought thousands, if not millions, more to the brink of extinction. While we can not (or should not) bring back those species already lost, and many others will likely be lost before we have a chance to save them, we are capable of saving many more. This is the work of Conservation Biologists the world over. In this course we will explore both the causes and effects of our impact on the planet, as well as what action can and are being taken to reduce the loss in biodiversity as much as possible. We will look at current research, projects, but also legislation, aimed at saving as much of our planets biosphere as we can.
selectedCourseReview.contribution: studies biodiversity conservation as an ecological component of environmental decisions

selectedCourseReview.name: Dynamic Earth
selectedCourseReview.actualContent: This course introduces you to the broad field of Earth Science. Earth Science in general and in all its sub disciplines is a very exciting and relevant field. You will never look at mountains, rivers and oceans in the same way after taking this course. You will discover in this course that many of the natural phenomena observed on (surface) and in (deep) the earth, are linked to processes of our Earth, that contrary to many other planets, is alive! The number of opportunities for employment in this field is increasing, because water, soil, mineral and fossil resources are limited. To limit the environmental impacts of our human endeavors new approaches are needed to counter water-soil-air pollution. Also, more efforts are needed to address the effects of the seemingly increased frequency of earthquakes, flooding, tsunamis and hurricanes. While studying the common geological phenomena, we will browse through major sub disciplines such as structural geology, mineralogy, petrology, earth history, geochemistry, geophysics, climatology, environmental geology, geohydrology, sedimentology, and resource management. Each one of these sub disciplines could easily fill a semester. At universities these sub-disciplines are usually taught by several professors that have specialized in one of the sub-disciplines. This course will be taught by professors partly based on the main division in Earth Science (surface earth disciplines) and Geophysics. Since geology is a typical outdoor science, you will not have a complete introduction without outdoor studies.
selectedCourseReview.contribution: introduces Earth processes and resources that shape human environments

selectedCourseReview.name: Natural Hazards, Risks & Adaptations
selectedCourseReview.actualContent: Covers geoscience principles and analytical tools to understand natural disasters. Compares risks from climate change‑driven events and mining disasters and teaches actions to reduce risks from events like earthquakes, droughts and toxic algae blooms.
selectedCourseReview.contribution: analyses hazards, climate risks and adaptation affecting settled places

selectedCourseReview.name: Earth Observation
selectedCourseReview.actualContent: This course serves as a 200-level elective within the Environmental Science unit of the Environment and Sustainability Cluster. Geospatial data and images from satellites or drones are widely used to explore and model changes in the Earth’s system at various scales. This course focused on hands-on experience with GIS and data integration techniques. We will explore, visualize, and analyze how human actions can impact global ecosystems and climate, and how tools like ArcGIS pro can promote sustainable practices like soil/water governance and coastal protection planning by combining data from different fields. This course includes practical exercises, a final exam and a case study based on earth science-focused research question.
selectedCourseReview.contribution: uses satellite and drone imagery and GIS to map human impacts and environmental change at several scales

selectedCourseReview.name: Earth System Science Tools
selectedCourseReview.actualContent: Explores interactions among biosphere, hydrosphere, lithosphere and atmosphere. Teaches system modelling, uses proxies and isotope tracers to study past and future climates and includes a field trip focused on greenhouse gas pathways.
selectedCourseReview.contribution: models Earth-system interactions, greenhouse gases and climate pathways

selectedCourseReview.name: Environmental Biogeochemistry
selectedCourseReview.actualContent: This course focusses on the biogeochemical processes on the earths surface. Most are related to soil-mineral-rock water interactions under near Earth -surface conditions. Biological and chemical controls on mineral formation processes will be studied in further detail as well as adsorption and leaching of nutrients or metals. Furthermore, (waste) -water treatment and engineered processes to recover valuable resources from waste, as well as some anthropogenic resource cycles are topics of this course. The theoretical and practical knowledge taught in SCIEART201/202 will be supplemented by using advanced geochemical modeling tools such as G eochemist Workbench. This course is very suitable for students in chemistry, geology and environmental science. The course may include some simple lab experiments, furthermore (in-class) exercises, one quiz and a case study.
selectedCourseReview.contribution: examines surface geochemistry, nutrient and metal cycles and water treatment, adding environmental-science depth

selectedCourseReview.name: Earth's Resources
selectedCourseReview.actualContent: Provides in‑depth geoscience research into resource and environmental challenges such as nuclear waste storage, geothermal energy and CO₂ capture. Students conduct literature reviews and produce class reports for presentation to a professional conference.
selectedCourseReview.contribution: studies resources and their environmental management, a scientific complement to spatial governance

selectedCourseReview.name: Sustainability Essentials I
selectedCourseReview.actualContent: ENSGATE101 - Sustainability Essentials serves as the Gateway course to all 200 level courses in the Environment and Sustainability Cluster. For that purpose we will discuss the tools and knowledge you need to follow and enjoy all 200 level course in the cluster. We will use the model of planetary boundaries to discuss the concepts of sustainability with an anthropogenic focus. The planetary boundaries concept was presented in 2009 and provides a novel synthesis of the most pertinent global environmental challenges by analysing the risk of crossing critical thresholds in the behaviour of the Earth system’s processes. These boundaries act as a framework to define a "safe operating space for humanity," highlighting the limits within which human development can occur without causing catastrophic harm to the planet. 3
selectedCourseReview.contribution: introduces planetary boundaries and human impacts, framing environmental change and sustainability

selectedCourseReview.name: Sustainability Essentials II
selectedCourseReview.actualContent: ENSGATE201 - Sustainability Essentials II serves as the Gateway course to several 300 level courses in the Environment and Sustainability Cluster. For that purpose we will discuss the tools and knowledge you need to follow and enjoy these course in the cluster. We will focus on three main topics (Waves, Chemistry and Material science) and on how they relate to Sustainability. You will have the opportunity to explore the topics in individual reflective journals as well as a project at the end of the course. In the project, you will use what you learned to analyse and discuss green washing. 3
selectedCourseReview.contribution: extends sustainability study through materials, chemistry and project work as preparation for technical environmental courses

selectedCourseReview.name: Climate Change
selectedCourseReview.actualContent: Climate change is the defining challenge of our time. It has large impacts on both the living and non-living Earth systems, as well as drives a number of profound societal transformations. This course is roughly divided in 3 parts. First, we will first focus on the drivers of anthropogenic climate change and its impacts on the natural world. Topics discussed include (but are not limited to) the properties of greenhouse gases, sea level rise, ocean acidification, climate feedback loops and effects on various biome types. Secondly, we will discuss impacts on various aspects of society. Topics discussed include (but are not limited to) food production, transportation, construction, health, and migration patterns. We will discuss climate governance and -justice. We will also look at the history of the climate change debate and identify strategies that have been deployed by interest groups to sow doubt and misinformation. Lastly, we will look into solutions for both adaptation and mitigation, such as renewable energy systems, carbon dioxide storage and climate-adaptive spatial planning. The course will include a number of guest lectures and excursions. After taking the course, you will be able to explain the fundamentals of climate change science. You will also be able to navigate a vast flow of information on climate change, and identify main and reliable sources; you will have insight in main climate change issues and have an overview of the pathways to mitigation and adaptation.
selectedCourseReview.contribution: links causes and impacts of climate change with societal transformations, governance and justice

selectedCourseReview.name: Life Cycle Analysis & Circular Economy
selectedCourseReview.actualContent: To prepare our society for a circular and sustainable future, we need to evaluate the environmental impact of products, processes, or services throughout their entire lifecycle, from raw material extraction to final disposal, or ideally re-usage as new raw materials. To do this, we have to understand the environmental, social and health consequences of products and processes and develop a strategic planning for future activi- ties. ENSSUST112 - Life Cycle Analysis & Circular Economywill be heavily focussed on “learning by doing”, rather than by just studying books. Therefore most of this course will consist of analysing different products, processes and services and include guest lectures by experts working in the field of sustainability and circularity. 3
selectedCourseReview.contribution: uses life-cycle analysis to evaluate environmental and social effects of products and circular interventions

selectedCourseReview.name: Renewable System Design
selectedCourseReview.actualContent: Teaches assessment of energy usage patterns and strategies for reducing consumption or transitioning to cleaner energy. Explores solar, wind and bioenergy solutions and includes technical and economic analysis; students deliver a report and presentation to a partner company.
selectedCourseReview.contribution: evaluates energy demand and renewable system design in the sustainability transition

selectedCourseReview.name: Research in a Sustainable Delta
selectedCourseReview.actualContent: In this project course you will work in small teams of two or three students on a research problem relevant for sustainability in the broadest sense. We are looking for collaborations with local companies and other institutions. The research questions are supplied by a regional institution or company that is active in areas related to sustainability in the broadest sense. In this way it is guaranteed that the research projects are indeed relevant for the Zeeland delta. Furthermore, students will have access to expertise and/or facilities of the external partner, which will broaden their perspective. Usually, there will be one person affiliated with the external partner organization involved with a project team as external advisor.
selectedCourseReview.contribution: conducts a project on a regional sustainability question with an external partner in the Zeeland delta

selectedCourseReview.name: Law, Society & Justice
selectedCourseReview.actualContent: This course offers three different perspectives on the law: the legal, the social and the normative. We spend the first part of the course exploring the definitions of law and the different understandings of law in a general sense. We take a brief look at the different legal systems of the world, and we discuss various fields of law: constitutional law, administrative law, criminal law, international law and human rights, as well as select fields of private law including property law, contract and torts law. After the Fall break, students consider the relationships between law and society and the concept of justice. In addition to reading and discussing the main principles within each field of law, we explore these through reading case law and performing trial simulations.
selectedCourseReview.contribution: introduces social and legal institutions as a prerequisite to studying European law in spatial governance

selectedCourseReview.name: Foundations of European Union Law
selectedCourseReview.actualContent: EU law is everywhere, from the very strict new rules on data-protection that literally pop-up with every website you open, to less apparent instances such as the EU rules on reducing plastic bags that have found their way into distinct and different national laws throughout the EU. European law by now significantly affects the legal order in European countries and reflects as well as shapes the process of European integration in multiple ways. This course introduces you to the EU legal order by familiarizing you first with the institutional framework of the European Union and the organization of its legal foundations in particular. We will then survey the key substantive areas of EU law that revolve around EU fundamental rights, citizenship, and the freedom of movement of persons, workers, goods and establishments. You will be equipped to understand the EU legal order and research its manifestations both at the EU level as well as in the domestic context in which most of the EU law manifests itself in the lives of citizens, consumers, businesses and governments. There will also be guest lectures to further illustrate EU law and its functioning in theory and practice. The course is divided in two main parts. In the first part we will jointly examine the procedural aspects of EU law through a combination of brief lectures, in-class exercises and discussions. In the second part we will study the substantive law of the EU through the method of Problem Based Learning. Students will study a relevant case using the seven-step PBL method.
selectedCourseReview.contribution: examines EU legal order and cross-border policy, relevant to European environmental governance without specialising in planning law

selectedCourseReview.name: Foundations of Comparative Politics
selectedCourseReview.actualContent: All over the world people seem increasingly dissatisfied with the way their political system works, whether its citizens in Bangladesh who ousted the Hasina government, or voters in consolidated democracies like Sweden who are increasingly voting for parties at the left and right extremes of the political spectrum. How can we understand and explain these developments? Foundations of comparative politics provides you with the key analytical tools to analyze and compare political systems and the development and functioning of democracies in particular. This is done using the research tools of ‘mainstream’ political science: theory driven qualitative and quantitative empirical research that seeks to describe and/or explain political phenomena. The course provides an overview and analysis of the core structures and institutions of political systems by examining the position of the state and studying its internal structures and functioning and its interaction with society. We examine these issues using the conceptual toolbox of comparative politics. We familiarize ourselves with the basic institutions that make up political institutions, and the way democracies and authoritarian regimes develop and can break down. We examine the functioning of consolidated democracies and the challenges they face from developments such as the decline of political parties, mediatization, the rising importance of non- majoritarian institutions such as courts and impact of globalization and internationalization on the capacity of domestic governments to act.
selectedCourseReview.contribution: provides comparative tools for analysing political systems and public decisions

selectedCourseReview.name: Theory of International Relations
selectedCourseReview.actualContent: Brewing wars in the South China Sea, the Middle East, and Europe, trade wars, global climate change, amongst a plethora of other crises and difficulties, show the importance of understanding International Relations and geopolitics. This course gives the student a basic understanding of International Relations through a historical and contemporary scope. You work with a textbook to understand the different schools of thought within International Relations and then use historical or contemporary topics to apply these theories to. This will be achieved by group presentations. Your knowledge will be further increased by homework assignments and an exam. Finally, you end the course with a United Nations Security Council Simulation, where you take on the role of one of the UNSC members, and plead your country’s case in a current problem of international relations.
selectedCourseReview.contribution: analyses international relations, geopolitics and cross-border processes

selectedCourseReview.name: European Union Politics
selectedCourseReview.actualContent: This course introduces you to the European Union, a body politic that has been characterized as diverse as Unidentified Political Object, an unimperial empire as well as a superstate. Whatever its nickname , the EU is as political as any other body invested with public authority. For political scientists this means that it is vital to understand its functioning and to see where power is exercised and how various state and non-state interests try to get their preferences turned into policies. In the first part of the course we outline key actors, institutions and decision -making rules and show how political scientists have employed various ways to study EU politics and policy- making. Students will engage in Navigating the EU exercises that show them EU politics in the making and the sources to be used for that. In the second part of the course we will more directly examine the clash of interests through a group based research project where you study a legislative dossier and the interaction between interest groups and Members of the European Parliament, using the E Us transparency register . A key focal point in this analysis concerns the relative power of business interests vis a vis other interests in EU - decisionmaking and assessing what this implies for the legitimacy and effectiveness of EU - policies.
selectedCourseReview.contribution: examines European Union actors and decisions that shape policy across borders

selectedCourseReview.name: Introduction to Sociology
selectedCourseReview.actualContent: Sociology provides a diverse and intricate toolkit composed of concepts, methods, and theories, which aids in comprehending and dissecting the functioning of societies on a local scale and the complex interconnections triggering global phenomena. Unlike disciplines like economics or political science, the subject of sociological inquiry is less clearly de fined. It encompasses all facets of human engagement within society, spanning from everyday interactions to the most longstanding social institutions. As a result, the wealth of knowledge within sociology can feel daunting, leaving one uncertain about where to begin. The course follows the recommendations 3 of the Sociological Literacy Framework 1, which is composed of the essential concepts and competencies in the discipline, as portrayed in the following table: Furthermore, this course overviews some of the most impactful sociological theories, including those by Marx, Weber, Durkheim, and Du Bois. It recognizes the social and historical backdrop that shaped these “classical” sociological ideas and concepts, notably influenced by imperialism and colonialism. This historical context notably sidelined the voices of BIPOC (Black, Indigenous, and People of Color) and women. Consequently, fundamental concepts like race and gender received inadequate theoretical attention within “classical” sociology. To bridge this gap, the course will prioritize students ’ interests and intellectual needs.
selectedCourseReview.contribution: introduces social structures and local-to-global interactions relevant to the human geography of communities

selectedCourseReview.name: Qualitative Research Methodology
selectedCourseReview.actualContent: Similar to their quantitative counterparts, qualitative researchers ask basic, but demanding, questions before they start making any enquires, e.g. What is truth? What is reality? What is knowledge? Why do we want to conduct research? What do we want to get out of it? In contrast to quantitative studies, however, qualitative researchers are less interested in numbers, trends and generalisations. Instead, they are keen to explore the messiness of social processes: what motivates people to take actions, how people make sense of their world, and how politics, history and cultures influence people’s thinking and actions. In this course, we will critically examine the four key stages of conducting qualitative research: (1) research design and preparation; (2) data collection and management; (3) data analysis and interpretation, and (4) research dissemination. Throughout the course, students are expected to take an active role – to form a research group and choose a research topic, to interrogate qualitative research theories and their own research experiences, and to critically reflect the research processes and students’ own positionality, biases and assumptions. At the end of the course, students will share their research findings and experiences with one another.
selectedCourseReview.contribution: teaches qualitative design, collection and interpretation for social and place-based inquiry

selectedCourseReview.name: Modern Sociology
selectedCourseReview.actualContent: Examines the trajectory of sociology within the culture of imperialism and colonial responses. Studies leading social theories and debates about modernity and critically engages with sociological discourses.
selectedCourseReview.contribution: explores colonial modernity and global social theory as a framework for changing societies

selectedCourseReview.name: Social Movements & Environmental Justice
selectedCourseReview.actualContent: Focuses on social movement theories and environmental justice. Uses case studies from the Environmental Justice Atlas and integrates perspectives such as feminism, anti‑colonialism, degrowth and environmental peacebuilding to encourage civic engagement.
selectedCourseReview.contribution: examines environmental justice movements and unequal effects of environmental decisions

selectedCourseReview.name: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
selectedCourseReview.actualContent: The course ‘GOSSOCI311 New Issues in Contemporary Sociology’ builds upon the topics covered in ‘GOSSOCI101 Introduction to Sociology’ and ‘GOSSOCI202 Modern Sociology’. Its primary goal is to familiarise students with significant debates in sociological theory from a global perspective. This edition of the course focuses specifically on the idea of civil society, examining topics such as solidarity, social capital, social trust, the public and civil sphere, and civil repair in modern societies. The first part of the course explores a critical approach to civil society, starting with Gramsci’s ideas, followed by Habermas’s ideas on the public sphere and Fraser’s critique. It will examine cases in the Global South, and we will watch and discuss a movie about the power of grassroots civil society. The second part focuses on Alexander’s work on the Civil Sphere, cases of civil repair in Latin America, and performances of solidarity with migrants along Europe's southern border. The final part will explore the decolonial critique of the classical approaches to civil society and the civil sphere. Alongside the theoretical component, the course also includes an empirical aspect. Students will select an NGO, voluntary organisation, or other Civil Society Organisation (CSO) to explore the concepts covered in the course and the challenges associated with the work undertaken by these organisations. Using a Community Engaged Learning (CEL) approach, students will observe and study an organisation throughout the semester to gain an understanding of its culture, impact, and challenges.
selectedCourseReview.contribution: studies civil society and social trust, relevant to place-based collective action and governance
